`tryFrom` returns null for an unknown value, and `var_export(null, true)` is `NULL`.
exercises.solution: `Size::Large->name` is `Large` and `->value` is `L`, printed next to each other. `tryFrom("M")` finds no case and returns `null`, which `var_export` writes as `NULL`. Output: `LargeL NULL`.

exercises.prompt: A search page reads a `?sort=` parameter from the URL and turns it into a `SortOrder` backed enum. Which is the best approach?

options.label: `SortOrder::tryFrom($_GET['sort'] ?? '') ?? SortOrder::Relevance`
options.feedback: Yes. An unknown or missing value falls back to a sensible default instead of crashing the page.

options.label: `SortOrder::from($_GET['sort'])`
options.feedback: Not yet. Anyone can type any value into a URL. `from` throws a `ValueError` for unknown values, and a missing parameter also produces a warning.

options.label: `constant("SortOrder::" . $_GET['sort'])`
options.feedback: Not yet. That looks up a case by its *name* using raw input, throws for unknown names, and invites people to probe your code's identifiers.

options.label: Use the string directly and skip the enum.
options.feedback: Not yet. Then every later use has to re-check the string, and a typo anywhere goes unnoticed.

hints: Input from a URL can be anything, or missing.
Which method returns null instead of throwing?
exercises.solution: Treat user input as untrusted: `tryFrom` returns `null` for anything that is not a valid value, `?? ''` handles a missing parameter, and the final `??` picks a default. Use `from` only where an unknown value means corrupted data that should stop the program.

hints: Follow the cycle: Red, then Green, then Amber, then Red …
exercises.solution: Starting at Red: 1 → Green, 2 → Amber, 3 → Red, 4 → Green. The cycle has length 3, so four steps land one step past the start: `Green`.

feedback.message: Not yet. `==` on two objects of the same class compares their properties.
Not yet. `===` on objects asks whether they are the same instance.

hints: `$c = $a` copies a handle, so `$c` and `$a` are the same instance.
exercises.solution: `$a == $b` compares properties (both 1, 2), so `true`. `$a === $b` asks whether they are the same object, and they are two separate instances, so `false`. `$c` holds a handle to the same object as `$a`, so `$a === $c` is `true`.

exercises.prompt: Using the lesson's `Money` class, `Money::of("10", Currency::EUR)->split(3)` returns three parts. What is the `minor` value (the number of cents) of the **first** part?

feedback.message: Close. 1000 cents do not divide evenly by 3; where does the leftover cent go?
Not yet. `minor` counts cents, and 10 euros is 1000 cents.

hints: 1000 = 3 × 333 + 1, and the remainder goes to the first parts.
exercises.solution: `intdiv(1000, 3)` is 333 with remainder 1. The first `remainder` parts get one extra cent, so the parts are 334, 333 and 333 cents, which add up to exactly 1000. The first is **334**.

exercises.prompt: `Invoice` implements `HasId` but not `Named`. Which parameter type accepts an `Invoice`?

options.label: `HasId|Named`
options.feedback: Yes. A union accepts anything that matches at least one member, and an `Invoice` is a `HasId`.

options.label: `HasId&Named`
options.feedback: Not yet. An intersection requires both interfaces, and `Invoice` has no `name()`.

options.label: `(HasId&Named)|null`
options.feedback: Not yet. This accepts an object with both interfaces, or null. An `Invoice` is neither.

hints: `|` means "any of these"; `&` means "all of these".
exercises.solution: A union type (`|`) is satisfied by any one of its members, so `HasId|Named` accepts an `Invoice`. An intersection (`&`) needs every member, so `HasId&Named` and the DNF type built from it both reject it.

feedback.message: Not yet. That is what `DateTimeImmutable` would give. `DateTime::modify` changes the object it is called on.

hints: `DateTime::modify` changes the object itself and returns it.
exercises.solution: `addDay` receives a handle to the caller's `DateTime`, and `modify` changes that object in place. So `$start` itself moved to 2 March, and the program prints `2026-03-02 2026-03-02`. With `DateTimeImmutable`, `modify` returns a new object and `$start` would stay on 1 March.
